scenario: You are the contracting officer on a competitive tradeoff source selection for 3,000 widgets, Government estimate $16.5M. Three proposals arrive. Offerors A and C are priced within 10% of the estimate, but both drew initial technical ratings of Marginal — neither demonstrated an adequate approach to the requirements. Offeror B is priced 40% above the estimate with an initial technical rating of Unacceptable: a deficiency-riddled proposal that is unawardable as written.

frameworks.why: The range comprises the most highly rated proposals — a formal PCO determination, SSA-approved, documented in the CRDD with reasons for inclusion and exclusion.

Nobody is cleanly awardable, so discussions are how the Government gets to an award: each offeror in the range must hear its own significant weaknesses and deficiencies with enough substance to respond.

baits: "Award without discussions to the least-bad offeror" — no initial proposal supports a clean award
"Keep B in the range out of caution" — an unawardable proposal priced 40% high has to earn inclusion, not inertia
key_moves: No proposal supports award as submitted — establish a competitive range and open discussions
Include A and C (Marginal is fixable through meaningful discussions); document B's exclusion in the CRDD on ratings AND price
Conduct meaningful discussions with A and C — each hears its own weaknesses and deficiencies, tailored, even-handed
Request FPRs after discussions close, re-evaluate, and select on the stated criteria

follow_ups.q: Offeror B demands to stay in — 'you can't eliminate us before discussions.' Can you?
follow_ups.h: The range is the most highly rated proposals — is B among them on any honest reading?
follow_ups.d: Yes, you can exclude B. The competitive range comprises the most highly rated proposals — an unawardable technical rating combined with a price 40% above the estimate keeps B out on both dimensions, documented in the CRDD signed by the CO and SSA. B is entitled to a pre-award debrief explaining its exclusion; it is not entitled to discussions the range determination lawfully denied it.

follow_ups.q: During discussions, Offeror A asks how their price compares to the competition. What can you say?
follow_ups.h: Discussions address their weaknesses — whose information would a price comparison reveal?
follow_ups.d: You can tell A their price appears high or low relative to the Government's analysis if that's a documented concern — but never reveal other offerors' prices, rankings, or relative standing. Discussions are about each offeror's own proposal. Disclosing competitive standing crosses into conduct that taints the selection: it's source selection information, and sharing it invites both a PIA problem and a protest from whoever the disclosure disadvantaged.

script: This is an RFO Part 15 source-selection question — the competitive-range decision. My help: the SSEB's documented evaluations, Legal, and the SSA who approves the range. The rule: no initial proposal supports award — two Marginals and an Unacceptable — so award without discussions is off the table even if the solicitation preserved it. I'd establish the competitive range on the most-highly-rated standard: A and C are in — Marginal with fixable weaknesses is exactly what meaningful discussions exist to cure; B is out on ratings and price together, documented in the CRDD. Then discussions with A and C — each hears its own significant weaknesses and deficiencies, tailored and even-handed — followed by FPRs, re-evaluation, and a tradeoff decision on the stated criteria. The panel wants the sequence: range, discussions, FPRs, award — each step on the record.

scenario: A board member leans back and asks: "What can Air Force Contracting do to combat the threat of China catching up to — and in some areas surpassing — USAF capabilities?"
ask: There's no framework to recite here — the panel wants your perspective as a business leader. What do you say?
key_moves: Speed as a weapon: every month cut from acquisition lead time is capability fielded sooner — use the streamlined authorities we already own (commercial procedures, OTs, CSOs, the RFO's trimmed process) instead of defaulting to the long way
Broaden the base: nontraditionals, commercial tech, and small business bring the innovation velocity the threat demands — the tools exist; the habit is what's missing
Buy like a portfolio: data rights and modular strategies that keep competition alive across a system's life, so we're never hostage to one vendor's pace
Develop people: COs who know the full toolkit make speed decisions confidently; training and warrants are combat capability
Protect the industrial base and supply chain — know where the single points of failure are before the crisis finds them

follow_ups.q: Which one of those would you actually change first in your own office, and how?
follow_ups.h: Pick something inside a PCO's actual authority — not policy you'd wish for.
follow_ups.d: Strong answers pick a lever the speaker actually controls: defaulting to commercial procedures and existing vehicles before building bespoke contracts; setting internal cycle-time standards for routine actions; pre-negotiating BPAs and ordering structures against recurring demand; or building the office's OT/CSO muscle through one deliberate pilot. The panel is testing whether your strategic view survives contact with your own signature block — answer with something you could start Monday.

follow_ups.q: Which acquisition authorities do you see as underused today — and what's the risk of overusing them?
follow_ups.h: Name the agility lanes, then show you know their discipline.
follow_ups.d: Underused: commercial-first determinations, existing vehicles before bespoke contracts, OTs and CSOs for genuinely nontraditional work, and the RFO's streamlined procedures used as designed. The overuse risk is the mirror image: agility lanes used to dodge discipline — an OT to skip competition, a CSO stretched past its purpose — which burns the authority for everyone when it fails review. The board wants both halves: eagerness to use the toolkit, and the judgment that every authority survives scrutiny only when used for its actual purpose.

script: This is a perspective question — the panel is testing whether I think like a business leader, not whether I can recite. I'd anchor on speed and breadth. Speed: our adversary's advantage is decision-to-fielding velocity, and contracting owns a controllable slice of that timeline — so my office defaults to the fastest lawful lane: commercial procedures, existing vehicles, OTs and CSOs where they genuinely fit, and the RFO's streamlined process used as designed. Breadth: the innovation we need lives partly outside the traditional base — nontraditionals and small business come in through the authorities built for them. Underneath both: data rights and modular strategies that keep competition alive for a system's whole life, and people trained to use the full toolkit confidently. China isn't out-regulating us — it's out-pacing us. Contracting's contribution to the fight is tempo.

scenario: The board president asks: "What does innovation mean to you — and how will you push innovative practices into your programs once you're an Unlimited PCO?"
ask: Answer in your own voice — the panel wants your working definition and your concrete plan, not a poster slogan.
key_moves: Define it operationally: innovation is fielding a better outcome faster — a business-process result, not a technology buzzword
Name your tools: commercial preference, OTs and CSOs where they fit, performance-based requirements that buy outcomes instead of tasks, modular strategies that keep options open
Make risk explicit: innovation means taking deliberate, documented business risk — the file explains the judgment, and my warrant exists to sign for it
Push it downward: train the team to bring me options, not just compliance — the question 'what would faster look like?' asked on every strategy
One concrete habit: every new requirement gets a genuine commercial-first and existing-vehicle look before anyone drafts a bespoke solicitation

follow_ups.q: Give the panel one example where innovation would be the WRONG answer.
follow_ups.h: Think about where the boring tool is the right tool — mature requirements, stable markets.
follow_ups.d: Strong answers show judgment about fit: a mature, stable, well-priced production requirement wants an FFP contract and disciplined administration, not a novel instrument; a routine severable service wants the base-plus-options rail. Innovation spent where a proven tool fits adds risk without return — the discipline is matching the instrument to the uncertainty, and 'boring on purpose' is often the most professional answer in the room. Panels reward candidates who know when NOT to reach for the shiny authority.

follow_ups.q: How do you create room for your people to take smart risks?
follow_ups.h: Cover, documentation, and what happens after a miss.
follow_ups.d: Three moves: give cover — the PCO owns the decision, so the team knows a defensible judgment call won't be re-litigated onto them; demand documentation — the file tells the story of the judgment, which converts 'risk' into 'reasoned decision'; and debrief misses without blame — a documented, reasonable call that didn't work is training material, not a career event. Innovation dies in offices where the only safe answer is the slowest one; it lives where judgment is expected, papered, and defended.

script: This is a perspective question, and I'd answer it as a definition plus a plan. My definition: innovation in contracting is fielding a better outcome faster — it's a business result, not a gadget. The plan, as an Unlimited PCO: first, defaults — every requirement gets a real commercial-first and existing-vehicle look before anyone builds bespoke; second, the right authorities used for their actual purpose — OTs and CSOs where nontraditional participation or prototype speed genuinely needs them, never as rule-avoidance; third, requirements shaped as outcomes so industry can propose the how. And underneath it: deliberate, documented risk-taking — my warrant exists so someone can sign for professional judgment, and my file will always show the judgment. The other half of the answer is knowing when innovation is wrong: mature production wants boring, disciplined FFP. Matching the tool to the uncertainty — that's the craft.

scenario: A panel member notes: "The rules are changing faster than they ever have — the RFO rewrite, class deviations landing monthly, thresholds moving, NDAA sections taking effect mid-year. What's right one day is wrong the next." She asks how you, as a contracting officer, stay current — and how you keep your team from acting on stale guidance.
ask: What are some concrete things you do to stay abreast of changes that affect your acquisitions?
key_moves: Primary sources on a rhythm: the live RFO text and class deviation lists at acquisition.gov, DPC memos, and the Federal Register — checked on a schedule, not when convenient
Never quote a threshold or citation from memory — verify against the current text before it goes in a document; the reg you memorized may have moved

Structured team mechanisms: a recurring policy touchpoint in staff meetings, routing significant changes with a one-line 'what this changes for us,' and updating office templates the week a change lands
Your network as an early-warning system: policy shop, Legal, peer COs across the enterprise — most changes announce themselves in conversation before they bite in a file
Treat currency as a professional obligation: the appendix of every guide rots — the habit of verification is what doesn't

follow_ups.q: A change lands mid-acquisition — the threshold your strategy relied on moved. What do you actually do with the active file?
follow_ups.h: Effective dates and applicability rules decide — which actions does the change actually reach?
follow_ups.d: First, read the change's own applicability terms: most changes apply to actions initiated (or contracts awarded) after an effective date, and many expressly grandfather in-flight actions — the answer is usually in the deviation or rule itself. Then document the analysis in the file: which version governs this action and why. If the change genuinely reaches your acquisition, adjust the strategy deliberately — amend the solicitation, re-approve at the right tier — rather than hoping nobody notices. The file that explains its own regulatory baseline survives every audit that follows a rule change.

follow_ups.q: A teammate cites a threshold from memory in a J&A draft — what do you do?
follow_ups.h: The habit is the finding, not the number.
follow_ups.d: Verify the number against the live RFO text before the document moves — most thresholds shifted in October 2025, so memory is a known-bad source. Fix the document, then coach the habit: every number in every document gets verified at acquisition.gov against the current text and deviations, no exceptions. And check the office templates, because a stale template reproduces the same wrong number faster than any individual can. The specific threshold matters less than the discipline — that's what the panel is really asking about.

script: This is a professional-habits question, and I'd answer with my actual system. Primary sources on a rhythm: the live RFO text and the class-deviation list at acquisition.gov, DPC policy memos, and the Federal Register — on my calendar, not left to chance. A personal rule the current environment demands: I never quote a threshold or citation from memory; every number gets verified against the live text before it enters a document, because what I memorized last quarter may have moved. For the team: a standing policy touchpoint in staff meetings, significant changes routed with one line on what they change for us, and templates updated the week a change lands — stale templates are how offices act on dead guidance. And my network — policy shop, Legal, peer COs — is the early-warning system; most changes announce themselves in conversation before they bite a file. The rules will keep moving. The habit of verification is what stays.
